name: Nisarg Mehta
body:
A growing number of executives are coming to us after unsuccessful attempts to elevate their presence on LinkedIn by hiring external writers or agencies to articulate their voice. In most cases, this results not just in underperformance, but in outcomes that actively work "against their objectives".

In short: their standing would have been better preserved had they opted not to publish at all.

This observation may seem counterintuitive, yet it reflects a broader reality of today’s B2B communication environment.

Before allocating more time, budget, or external resources to LinkedIn, it is worth grounding in a few key principles:

1. We are living in an age of extreme overcommunication. Millions of pieces of content are produced each day, and advances in artificial intelligence have reduced the friction required to generate an endless stream of content. In such an environment, restraint carries more value than participation that is poorly conceived (i.e., misaligned with the brand it represents).

2. The underlying problem is not just a lack of effort. More often, it is a failure to begin in the right place. Most agencies and writers approach brand communication on LinkedIn as a publishing exercise. The process begins with the wrong premise: "What should we post today?" But brand communication starts with positioning: "Where and how you stand in the mind of your prospect."

At its simplest, it is the structured placement of aligned signals into a consistent frame until the market or prospect begins to associate you with a singular, high-value outcome. Positioning informs the narrative. The narrative shapes the message. Only then should individual pieces of communication take form. Reversing this sequence is the most common error and carries tangible consequences.

3. None of this suggests that marketing should be rigid. The most effective marketers routinely challenge conventions and reshape expectations. However, there are principles, and there are principles in practice. The best marketers understand how things work in practice. Know the rules so they can be applied intelligently.

4. Technical writing ability, while essential, is only one component of effective executive communication. At its highest level, executive communication sits at the intersection of strategy, positioning, and narrative discipline.

5. And here’s the thing… there isn’t really a fifth point. Remember the good old days of marketing when an "odd number of tips" was a rule? Well, the good old days of marketing are gone, and it no longer requires arbitrary symmetry.

name: Nisarg Mehta
body:
Business owners selling complex services or products often limit their growth when they mistake a single social platform for the entire buyer journey, rather than recognising it as one intentional component within a broader commercial system. Most do not realise the cost of that misunderstanding until pipeline momentum has slowed.

The recurring debate over whether LinkedIn, Instagram, Substack, or X is the 'best' platform misses the point entirely. Each can contribute to visibility and credibility. None, in isolation, constitutes a buyer journey.

One of the most common mistakes in B2B markets is optimising content for feed performance rather than buyer progression. These are fundamentally different objectives.

The more important discipline is signal interpretation.

Customer feedback, platform analytics, and market response are valuable inputs only when examined critically. Not every signal carries equal weight.

A focused, intentional channel mix, selected for its ability to influence the right stakeholders at the right stage of the buying process, will consistently outperform a broad but reactive presence.

Social media should function as a signal layer.

The conversion engine itself should be built elsewhere: through credible proof, substantive conversations, institutional trust, and a buying experience designed for considered decisions rather than momentary attention.

name: Nisarg Mehta
body:
Every time a B2B brand captures disproportionate market attention, commentary follows almost immediately.

Within 48 hours, the post-analysis begins.

The algorithm favored it. The timing aligned with distribution windows. The format reflected an emerging content pattern.

Each explanation is technically reasonable, but none of them is strategically instructive.

The more consequential variable is the ex-ante strategic thesis.

Why that positioning? Why that buyer persona? Why that framing? Why that timing?

This is where durable B2B marketing advantage actually resides: in pre-outcome strategic reasoning.

Before performance dashboards validate the decision, a strategist must determine which hypothesis deserves commitment.

If a marketing organization proceeds to execution without establishing this ex-ante strategic thesis, it is effectively deploying capital and creative assets without directional conviction.

If we are pursuing non-linear enterprise impact, the standard of thinking that precedes execution must also rise.

name: Nisarg Mehta
body:
What many founders (or marketing agencies) overlook is a foundational principle: before attempting to capture the attention of your target audience with a worn, manipulative hook, you must first establish alignment.

In practical terms, you must operate on the same wavelength as the person you intend to reach.

Association does the substantive work.

Every subject line, message, and campaign either strengthens the right associations or quietly erodes them.

Whether an email is opened or someone clicks 'see more' is secondary.

The more consequential question is one of strategic coherence.

If the majority of your audience does not experience your framing as intelligent, relevant, and contextually appropriate, you are effectively borrowing attention at the expense of brand equity.

Short-term curiosity is a fragile return.

The long-term cost is dilution of the associations that position you as credible, deliberate, and worth engaging.

name: Nisarg Mehta
body:
The prevailing advice on LinkedIn urges founders to build a founder-led brand.

The underlying observations are correct. The strategic conclusion most people draw from them is not.

When every post casts you as the hero, the prospect becomes a spectator.

In any effective narrative, there is only one hero.

If your objective is to move a prospect closer to a buying decision, that hero cannot be you. It must be them.

A founder-as-hero narrative becomes a profile piece.

A customer-as-hero narrative begins with the reader's problem, articulates the tension, and provides a framework for making a better decision.

You do not disappear. You shift from protagonist to guide.

You are not the one on the quest; you are the one with the map.

This positioning decision reshapes everything downstream.

name: Nisarg Mehta
body:
Last month, I reviewed the LinkedIn communication of a company that had published more than a hundred posts over six months.

Individually, many were insightful.

Yet despite the volume and quality, the communication failed to create meaningful influence.

Each post subtly positioned the company in a different mental category.

Every interaction with a prospect is a micro-commitment.

For that commitment to compound, two things must happen.

First, the reader must conclude: 'This is valuable.'

Second, they must give you permission to return.

Repetition, when coherent, creates structure.

Authority is simply the byproduct of consistently placing aligned signals into the same cognitive frame.

The common mistake is placing bricks into different buildings.

When a prospect lands on your profile, they should immediately associate you with one clear idea.

That is how positioning compounds over time.

name: Suvam Sahoo
body:
Over time, my understanding of what it truly means to build a company has changed completely.

Most people know me as someone who loves the process, the thrill of building and operating companies.

What fewer people know is that my philosophy around building has evolved dramatically.

There’s a saying I’ve come to believe:

"Busy founders are seldom great. Great founders are seldom busy."

And that evolution continues to shape how I build Knox today.

I once believed the founder was the company, the person who had to push hardest, hustle longest, and stay busiest.

But hard work, I’ve learned, is a function of both effort and value.

Effort is finite; it’s constrained by time.

Value, on the other hand, can expand infinitely when leveraged through systems and people.

In the early days, every founder does it all. You write the code, close the deals, fix the bugs, and take out the trash. It’s a necessary phase, but not a scalable one.

The pivotal shift happens when you hire people who are better than you at their craft, and then give them the trust and ownership to lead.

Because the true job of a CEO isn’t to do everything; it’s to make themselves increasingly replaceable. To continuously step out of roles and elevate their focus to the next level.

If your company needs you to function every day, then it stops when you do.

name: Suvam Sahoo
body:
Finding the right Shopify expert in India is not about availability. There is no shortage of talent. What there is, is a shortage of informed decisions.

Most businesses follow a familiar pattern: they post "Looking for a Shopify developer," receive dozens of responses, select the most confident candidate, and find themselves reassessing the decision a few months later when delivery falls short of expectations.

But the real issue is a lack of clarity around requirements.

Shopify is not a single discipline. The term "Shopify expert" is often too broad to be useful.

Here is my take on who to bring in based on your current stage and growth plans:

(1) Freelancers

Pros:
- Lower cost with flexible engagement terms
- Fast to onboard for short, well-scoped projects
- Direct communication with the person doing the work
- Wide availability across skill sets and budgets

Cons:
- Single point of failure
- Limited capacity for large projects
- No built-in project management or QA process
- Continuity risk on longer engagements

(2) Shopify Agencies

Pros:
- Dedicated team across design, development, QA, and strategy
- Better accountability and scalability
- Structured project delivery

Cons:
- Higher cost
- Quality varies significantly
- Some agencies rely on inexperienced resources

(3) In-House Developers

Pros:
- Deep understanding of your business
- Fast turnaround
- Long-term alignment
- Cost-efficient at scale

Cons:
- High ownership cost
- Hiring takes time
- Knowledge concentration risk
- Best suited for brands with ongoing development needs

Refer back to this before your next Shopify hiring decision.

name: Suvam Sahoo
body:
A question I hear very frequently from founders is:

"With so many tools and plugins available, what should be integrated from day one and what can wait?"

The answer is simpler than most expect.

In the early stages, your objective is not to build the most feature-rich storefront. Your objective is to create a buying experience that is clear, credible, and frictionless.

Founders often mistake app installations for progress.

What is essential from day one?

(1) Reliable payment infrastructure.

(2) Shipping and post-purchase communication.

(3) Foundational analytics.

A few things to avoid:

(i) Don't adopt an app-first mindset.

(ii) Don't scale features before demand.

(iii) Don't build based on assumptions.

The most effective ecommerce operators build for the customers they have today.

Remember: Master the basics. Complexity takes care of itself.

name: Suvam Sahoo
body:
India’s D2C market is growing very fast. Every month, many new brands are launched.

But when you look closely, a different picture appears.

Many new brands fail because they never find product-market fit.

One of the biggest mistakes founders make is believing India is one single market.

It is not.

India is made up of many different customer groups with different cultures, buying habits, price expectations, and preferences.

Another major problem is that too many brands are copying each other.

Most are selling similar products, using similar marketing, and targeting customers in the same way.

Before starting another brand in an already crowded category, founders should ask one important question:

What real customer problem still needs to be solved, and can we solve it better than others?

That is what strong positioning really means.

There are still hundreds of consumer problems waiting to be solved better.

That is what I hope to see more of in the years ahead: Indian brands growing into globally respected consumer companies.

name: Suvam Sahoo
body:
I recently chose to end a client engagement.

It is never a pleasant decision, but leadership is often defined by the choices others avoid.

What allows a business to endure through years of change, competition, and volatility? Direction.

Many operators dilute their advantage by chasing every opportunity.

The strongest businesses do the opposite.

They build around coherence.

If a project is misaligned, the answer is no.

We do not compromise standards for short-term revenue.

We believe in fairness at every level.

A business is only as strong as its team.

Some clients disregard timelines, demand endless revisions, or treat teams without respect.

When that happens, we disengage decisively.

Every founder faces this choice repeatedly: pursue everything, or protect what compounds.

Define your direction. Learn disciplined refusal. Work with aligned people. Protect your team.
